corpus.signal_text:
G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil, including diesel, amid energy crunch
Move would start with 'substantial' diesel release within first 20 days
The G7 nations said they agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with "substantial" amounts of diesel, after the fuel recently hit record prices in the United States.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on social media the diesel release would happen "immediately," echoing a G7 promise to start immediately with a "frontloaded substantial release" of diesel within the next 20 days and the rest over four months.
Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.
Gas and diesel prices have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there's no end in sight.
The average price of diesel in Canada was $2.63 per litre as of Thursday, though prices were higher in some cities, like Vancouver, where a litre of the fuel cost about $2.71. Heightened prices put pressure on transport truck drivers and farmers, who rely on diesel to run vehicles and equipment.
France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after videoconference talks that French President Emmanuel Macron presided over. The G7 countries are Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., plus EU representation.
The International Energy Agency will co-ordinate the effort to combat soaring fuel prices.
"We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels (MB) to begin immediately over 4 months, including a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners," the statement said.
The release follows a March announcement that International Energy Agency member countries would release 426 million barrels of oil and products to stabilize the oil market.
The move also comes after Trump last week floated the idea of banning diesel exports in hopes of bringing down gas prices for American drivers — a move experts caution could backfire, putting strain on an already-stretched global fuel market and further raising prices globally.

After increased pressure from Washington, the G7 held an emergency meeting on energy. The world's wealthiest nations say they will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel in their reserves.
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:
It seems President Trump has prevailed on the world's wealthiest nations to release diesel from their stockpiles. That decision came earlier today at an emergency G7 meeting. Trump had been threatening to stop all exports of U.S. diesel fuel if Europeans didn't release their own diesel. A U.S. ban would have pushed already high global diesel prices even higher. And those steep prices, which have risen substantially since the U.S. went to war with Iran, are already squeezing everyone, from farmers to small business owners. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley joins us now from Paris. Hi there.
ELEANOR BEARDSLEY, BYLINE: Good afternoon, Juana.
SUMMERS: Eleanor, tell us more about what the G7 decided today.
BEARDSLEY: Well, in this emergency meeting, they decided to release 100 million barrels over the next four months, beginning immediately, and they'll begin by releasing barrels of diesel fuel in the first 20 days. France chairs the G7, and President Emmanuel Macron convened the meeting by video conference, which included the head of the International Energy Agency, which is based in Paris.
Macron said the release would be coordinated by the IEA. Macron said G7 members would also coordinate to increase production and bring down transport costs like the insurance for tankers, he said, and push to get more tankers flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
SUMMERS: And, Eleanor, President Trump's earlier threat to cut off diesel fuel experts - did it work?
BEARDSLEY: Well, I would say, yes, that pressure did work, even though no one outright said so. You know, Europe is extremely dependent on imports of oil and diesel from the Middle East and the U.S., and its dependence has increased since Russia's war on Ukraine - because Russia no longer is a supplier - and since the Iran war and the choking of the Strait of Hormuz. Macron has called a possible U.S. diesel export ban, quote, "catastrophic." Just take France. It consumes about 600,000 barrels of diesel a day and imports half of that.
